strengths: The paper presents a simple, model-agnostic framework for measuring functional activation sparsity in non-ReLU Transformers, with an interpretable top-p rule and a clearly defined critical-sparsity metric.

The empirical study spans several model families and scales, four FFN activation locations, pretrained and instruction-tuned variants, multiple downstream tasks, and an initial diffusion-LLM experiment.
The component-wise findings—particularly the comparison of input, gate, up-projection, and intermediate activations—are potentially useful for researchers designing sparse-inference methods.
The manuscript is concise, well organized, and visually clear, and it openly acknowledges that moderate activation sparsity alone offers limited theoretical speedup.
weaknesses: The claimed universality is substantially stronger than the evidence. Experiments cover only three closely related open-model families, mostly English likelihood-based benchmarks, models up to 32B parameters, and FFN activations. Code, mathematics, multilingual tasks, long-context generation, modern reasoning evaluations, and substantially different architectures are absent.

The contribution is primarily an empirical characterization using magnitude pruning, a standard idea closely related to several cited activation-sparsity studies. The paper does not establish a sufficiently strong methodological or theoretical advance over prior work, nor does it provide controlled, matched comparisons with the principal existing sparsification methods.

Claims about practical acceleration are not validated with latency, throughput, memory traffic, kernel efficiency, or energy measurements. Dynamic top-p selection and unstructured masks can carry considerable overhead, so induced sparsity does not by itself demonstrate realizable acceleration. Some activation locations must also be computed before their masks are known, further limiting the practical interpretation.

The central metric mixes two phenomena: concentration of activation magnitudes and downstream robustness to perturbing intermediate representations. Without controls such as random pruning, fixed masks, structured pruning, or matched-norm noise, the results do not isolate activation sparsity as the cause of robustness.

The 99% critical-sparsity threshold is arbitrary and its estimate depends on an unspecified threshold grid. No confidence intervals, repeated measurements, sensitivity analysis, or uncertainty for the fitted scaling trends are reported. Averaging normalized accuracy across heterogeneous tasks can obscure important failures and make the threshold sensitive to baseline scores.

The training and scaling conclusions are observational and confounded. Model size changes together with depth, width, data, and training recipe, while pretrained versus instruction-tuned checkpoints differ in both training and task suitability. Extrapolating these limited trends to frontier or reasoning models is therefore speculative.

The diffusion-LLM result uses a single diffusion model and only a few tasks, which is insufficient to support a general claim about diffusion LLMs. Likewise, the recommendation that sparsification should be entirely data-free is not directly demonstrated against calibrated or trained alternatives under distribution shift.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: the exact top-p sweep, evaluation-harness version/configurations, task metrics and aggregation, checkpoint identifiers, numerical per-task results, compute requirements, and code availability are not clearly provided. There is also a dimensional inconsistency in the stated FFN matrix shapes under the displayed column-vector formulation.

The top-p framework is simple, model-agnostic, and easier to compare across heterogeneous activation vectors than a fixed top-k rule.
Comparing input, gate, up-projection, and intermediate activations is practically relevant and challenges the assumption that gates are necessarily the best sparsification target.
The paper is concise and generally understandable, and it reports numerical critical-sparsity values in addition to aggregate plots.
weaknesses: The central claim of a “universal property” is substantially overstated. The experiments cover only a few closely related dense decoder-only GLU architectures; they exclude MoE models, encoder or encoder-decoder models, reasoning models, and materially different architectures. The diffusion conclusion rests on one 8B model and a small task subset.

The claimed practical acceleration guidance is not validated with latency, throughput, memory-traffic, energy, or sparse-kernel measurements. Top-p selection itself requires magnitude computation and sorting/selection, whose overhead is ignored. Consequently, sparsity percentages cannot establish real speedups or that input sparsification is the most efficient approach.

There are no empirical comparisons against the principal existing activation-sparsity systems discussed in the paper. Comparing only top-p, top-k, and max-p masking does not substantiate claims of practical competitiveness, stronger acceleration, or advantages over calibrated and predictor-based methods.

The evaluation protocol is inadequately specified and statistically fragile. The paper omits task sample counts, harness/version details, checkpoint identifiers, decoding and diffusion settings, numerical precision, seeds, uncertainty estimates, and per-task baseline scores. “Critical sparsity” uses a hard 99% threshold on noisy accuracies, yet no confidence intervals or significance tests are supplied.

The paper acknowledges nonzero measured sparsity even at p=1 due to finite-precision accumulation around massive activations. Under the mathematical definition, p=1 should retain every nonzero coordinate. Leaving this implementation artifact unresolved raises concerns about the correctness of the masks and reported sparsities, especially because the central metric is derived from these masks.

Several conclusions go well beyond the evidence: modest-size trends are extrapolated to frontier models; task variation is used to argue against auxiliary-data calibration without directly measuring overfitting or transfer; and results on instruction-tuned and diffusion models are used to predict benefits for reasoning models without evaluating them.

The novelty is limited. Magnitude-based activation masking and activation-sparsity observations are established, while the main new contribution is primarily an empirical survey with a straightforward top-p rule. The paper provides little mechanistic explanation for why the reported patterns arise.

Reproducibility is weak: no code or artifact is identified, and essential implementation and evaluation details are missing. The unusually dense, nearly unreadable appendix heatmaps do not compensate for the absence of accessible underlying results.

The max-p optimization in Appendix B.1 is formally incorrect: requiring |v_i|m_i to exceed the threshold for every coordinate makes the constraint infeasible whenever an entry lies below the threshold. This further weakens confidence in the technical presentation.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically relevant question: whether functional activation sparsity exhibits consistent behavior across modern non-ReLU LLMs.

The empirical scope is relatively broad, covering multiple sizes from Gemma3, Llama3.1/3.2, and Qwen2.5; four FFN activation locations; pretrained and instruction-tuned variants; and one diffusion language model.
The top-p framework provides a simple, model-agnostic way to compare sparsity robustness without auxiliary training or calibration data. The comparison with top-k and max-p is useful.

Several findings are potentially valuable to practitioners, particularly the scaling trend, variation across tasks and training recipes, and the observation that input sparsification can match gate sparsification.
The paper is concise and well organized. Figures communicate the main trends effectively, and the appendix reports numerical critical-sparsity values for all principal models.
weaknesses: The main contribution is predominantly a descriptive empirical study built around a simple sparsification rule. Many underlying observations—functional sparsity, model/task dependence, and increasing redundancy with scale—are closely related to prior work, making the incremental novelty borderline for a top-tier venue.

The claims of universality and practical acceleration are substantially stronger than the evidence. Only three closely related GLU-based autoregressive model families and one diffusion model are studied; no attention components, MoE models, reasoning models, generation-quality evaluations, or frontier-scale models are evaluated.

There are no latency, throughput, memory-traffic, or energy measurements. Top-p selection itself requires magnitude computation and selection/sorting, while useful sparse execution depends heavily on hardware and kernels. Consequently, the claim that input sparsification is the most efficient approach is not established by sparsity percentages alone.

The critical-sparsity metric is sensitive to the threshold grid and evaluation noise, yet the paper does not report uncertainty, repeated runs, statistical tests, or confidence intervals. Defining the boundary as retaining 99% of baseline accuracy may be especially unstable when task estimates have finite-sample noise.

Important reproducibility details are missing or insufficiently explicit, including exact checkpoint identifiers, task configurations and sample sizes, lm-eval-harness version, evaluated top-p grid, decoding settings for LLaDA, hardware, and implementation overhead. No code or artifact availability is stated.

Several causal or prescriptive interpretations are insufficiently supported. Differences across tasks do not by themselves show that calibration methods overfit, and differences between pretrained and instruction-tuned checkpoints do not isolate training effects because their output behavior and baseline task performance also differ.
The diffusion-LLM result is narrow—one model, four tasks, and no end-to-end generation or speed evaluation—so it supports an initial observation rather than the broader acceleration conclusions.

The stated max-p optimization is formally incorrect: requiring |v_i|m_i >= p||v||∞ for every coordinate prevents setting below-threshold mask entries to zero when p is positive. This does not necessarily invalidate the experiment if the implementation used the intended thresholding rule, but it is a technical error that should be corrected.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem and provides a broad empirical study spanning three dense autoregressive model families, pretrained and instruction-tuned variants, a reasoning model, two mixture-of-experts models, and a diffusion language model.

The unified top-p intervention makes it possible to compare several FFN activation locations without retraining or model-specific calibration. The corresponding sparsity-performance curves are intuitive and practically informative.

The comparison among input, gate, up-projection, intermediate, and joint input/intermediate sparsification yields useful observations, particularly that input sparsification can be competitive with gate-based sparsification.
The diffusion-LLM experiments and analysis of mask similarity across denoising steps are relatively novel and identify an interesting direction for future acceleration work.
The paper is generally clear and well organized, and it supplies extensive per-family, per-task, layer-wise, and sparsification-rule results in the appendix.
weaknesses: The central critical-sparsity metric is statistically fragile. It is defined using a 1% performance tolerance, yet the paper reports no confidence intervals, paired bootstrap tests, repeated runs, or sample counts. On several finite benchmarks, a 1% change is comparable to evaluation noise or score granularity. Taking the highest passing point from a discrete threshold grid further makes the metric sensitive to noise, grid resolution, and non-monotonic curves.

The scaling claim is observational and overstated. Model size is confounded with width, depth, architecture, training data, and training recipe; Qwen results are visibly non-monotonic, the largest dense model is only 32B, and no uncertainty or statistical analysis of the fitted trends is given. Consequently, claims about universal behavior and future frontier models are not established.

The effective-rank evidence has a serious normalization confound. For an activation matrix with n tokens and dimension d, effective rank is at most min(n,d), but the paper divides it by d. If batch token counts are fixed or comparable while d grows, the normalized rank will mechanically decrease with model width. Batch sizes and token counts are not reported, so Figure 3b does not independently demonstrate increasing redundancy.

The paper motivates acceleration but evaluates neither end-to-end latency nor kernel-level speedups for the proposed intervention. Per-token top-p selection entails magnitude computation, selection/sorting, and dynamic unstructured masks; intermediate sparsification additionally assumes an oracle mask after much of the relevant computation has already occurred. Results from other sparsification systems do not establish that these particular masks yield practical speedups after their overheads.

Comparisons with prior methods are inadequate. Alternative top-k and max-p rules are tested, mostly on small models, but there is no controlled quantitative comparison against representative calibrated, predictor-based, gate-based, or input-pruning methods in sparsity, accuracy, and runtime. Claims that the approach reaches levels comparable to existing work and that input sparsification is the most practical method are therefore insufficiently supported.

Averaging normalized accuracy across heterogeneous tasks can hide severe task-specific regressions, even though the paper itself demonstrates substantial task dependence. A deployment-relevant operating point should account for worst-case or per-task constraints rather than defining safety through the average alone.

Several specialized experiments are too limited for their conclusions: reasoning is assessed using one 4B model pair and three tasks, while the diffusion comparison uses one diffusion model and only three directly compared tasks. The explanation that diffusion denoising causes greater tolerance is speculative rather than experimentally isolated.

Important reproducibility details are missing, including the exact threshold grid for all experiments, evaluation sample counts, generation and decoding settings, diffusion/Monte Carlo settings, seeds, and uncertainty estimates. The displayed code-release statement also contains no accessible repository location in the submitted manuscript.

The mathematical FFN notation gives projection-matrix shapes inconsistent with the stated column-vector multiplication, and some causal or prescriptive language—such as calling gate computation wasteful, advocating universally data-free methods, and attributing output-length changes to sparsity—is stronger than the evidence warrants.

strengths: The paper studies a timely efficiency question across a broad collection of dense, instruction-tuned, reasoning, mixture-of-experts, and diffusion language models.
The unified comparison of input, gate, up-projection, intermediate, and combined-input sparsification provides useful descriptive evidence about where FFN activations are most tolerant to pruning.
The diffusion-LLM experiments and analysis of mask similarity across denoising steps are relatively novel and may motivate more rigorous follow-up work.
The paper is generally readable, and it reports per-task results, exact aggregate sparsity values, and comparisons among several sparsification rules.
weaknesses: The central practical implication is not demonstrated. Top-p is an oracle-like, token-wise operation that examines activations and sorts or selects their magnitudes; the paper provides neither an efficient implementation nor latency, memory, kernel-overhead, or end-to-end speed measurements. High induced sparsity therefore does not establish useful acceleration, especially for dynamic unstructured masks.

The claimed scaling law or universal increase with model size is supported mainly by least-squares trend lines over very few, architecturally confounded model points. The Qwen results are visibly non-monotonic, no statistical tests or controlled scaling experiments are provided, and model size is entangled with depth, width, training data, baseline capability, and model family.

Critical sparsity is a fragile metric: it uses an arbitrary 1% threshold on noisy benchmark accuracies without confidence intervals, repeated runs, or significance testing. Taking the highest observed point can amplify evaluation noise and non-monotonicity, while averaging heterogeneous tasks can conceal substantial degradation on individual tasks.

The paper does not compare its proposed framework quantitatively against representative existing activation-sparsity methods in matched settings. Comparisons of top-p, top-k, and max-p do not replace baselines such as calibrated input pruning, gate-based methods, or learned predictors, so claims of practical superiority and guidance are insufficiently supported.

The MoE analysis is materially underspecified. It is unclear how a model-level accuracy threshold is converted into a separate critical sparsity for each expert, how rarely routed experts are handled, or whether routing frequency confounds the reported minima, maxima, and averages. This makes the expert-wise conclusions difficult to validate.

The diffusion and reasoning experiments omit important evaluation details such as decoding parameters, sample counts, stochastic variability, and generation-length controls. The acknowledged truncation of Qwen reasoning outputs is itself a confound, while the LLaDA–LLaMA comparison does not control for their different training objectives or dense baseline quality.

Several conclusions substantially exceed the evidence: three dense families, two MoE models, and one diffusion model do not establish universality; task-dependent sparsity does not imply that calibration necessarily overfits; and sparsification-induced robustness is repeatedly conflated with intrinsic activation sparsity.

Reproducibility is limited by missing implementation-level details, threshold-search resolution, task-specific metrics and sample sizes, and precise procedures for all-input, MoE, and diffusion experiments. The displayed code-release statement also does not provide an accessible repository link in the submitted manuscript.

strengths: Provides a clear, unified framework for measuring functional activation sparsity across different FFN activation locations without retraining or model-specific assumptions.
The empirical scope is unusually broad, covering multiple dense model families and scales, pretrained and instruction-tuned variants, reasoning models, two MoE models, and a diffusion language model.

The comparison among input, gate, up-projection, intermediate, and joint-input sparsification yields useful practical observations; in particular, the finding that input sparsification can rival gate sparsification is relevant to efficient inference research.
The diffusion-LLM experiments are novel and informative, including both sparsity tolerance and temporal mask-stability analyses.
The paper is well organized, clearly written, and includes useful appendices with exact critical-sparsity values, per-task results, and comparisons among sparsification rules.
weaknesses: The claimed scaling law and “universal” characterization are stronger than the evidence. Critical sparsity is not consistently monotonic within families—especially Qwen—and model size is confounded with architecture, training data, depth, width, and intermediate dimension. The fitted trends lack uncertainty or significance analysis.

The effective-rank evidence is potentially misleading: effective rank is computed on an n-by-d token-activation matrix and then divided by d. Because rank is bounded by the batch token count n, this normalization can mechanically decrease as model width d grows even without increased representational redundancy. Controls with matched dimensionality or token-to-width ratios are needed.

Critical sparsity is defined using an arbitrary 1% threshold and as the highest empirically observed sparsity satisfying it, but the paper does not report confidence intervals, repeated evaluations, statistical testing, or sensitivity to the threshold and top-p grid. Benchmark noise and non-monotonic accuracy fluctuations could materially affect this metric.

The work motivates acceleration but reports no end-to-end latency, memory, or kernel-level measurements. Per-token top-p selection itself entails norm computation and selection/sorting overhead, while dynamic unstructured sparsity may not translate cleanly into realized speedups. Thus the practical-efficiency conclusions rely heavily on prior work rather than the evaluated method.

Comparisons with existing activation-sparsification approaches are limited. Alternative masking rules are compared, but there is no direct quality-efficiency comparison against representative input-, gate-, or predictor-based baselines under matched conditions.

Several causal interpretations are speculative—for example, attributing diffusion models’ higher tolerance to their denoising process. The LLaDA–LLaMA comparison does not isolate generation paradigm from differences in training, objectives, and evaluation procedures.

Important reproducibility details are underspecified in the manuscript, including the exact top-p grid, evaluation sample counts, decoding settings, random seeds, harness version/configuration, and details of per-expert MoE measurement. A code release is asserted, but the anonymized manuscript provides no inspectable resource.
